Fourth Commandment
FORTH kuh-MAND-ment
noun phrase (biblical commandment)
From Old English feowertha (fourth, ordinal of four) + Late Latin commandamentum (commandment, from commandare, to commit, entrust, from com, together, + mandare, to order or entrust). The Fourth Commandment is the Sabbath commandment of Exodus 20:8–11: “Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy.” It is the longest of the ten, grounding the weekly pattern of rest and worship in the six-day pattern of creation and God's own seventh-day rest (Gen 2:2–3).

Biblical Definition

The Fourth Commandment commands Israel (and, in the Christian re-application, the church) to observe one day in seven as a holy rest dedicated to the worship of God, grounded in God's own rest on the seventh day of creation (Gen 2:2–3) and the redemptive rest he gave Israel from Egypt (Deut 5:15). The command is fourfold: (1) remember it (not neglect it from inattention), (2) keep it holy (set it apart from ordinary labor and commerce), (3) labor six days (the commandment sanctifies ordinary work as well as the day of rest), and (4) rest on the seventh (the Sabbath principle of cessation from ordinary labor). Exodus grounds the Sabbath in creation order; Deuteronomy grounds it additionally in redemption from Egyptian slavery. The New Testament applies the pattern christologically: Christ himself is Lord of the Sabbath (Matt 12:8); his resurrection on the first day of the week shifted the church's weekly observance from Saturday (the seventh day of the old creation) to Sunday (the eighth day, the first day of the new creation), a shift reflected in Acts 20:7 and 1 Corinthians 16:2. Hebrews 4:9 teaches that “there remains a Sabbath rest for the people of God” — pointing to the eschatological fulfillment of the commandment in the eternal rest of the new creation. The Reformed tradition, following Calvin and the Westminster Confession, regards the weekly day of rest as a creation ordinance binding on all humanity (not merely a ceremonial law for Israel), fulfilled not abolished in Christ, and re-applied to the Lord's Day as the Christian Sabbath.

Webster 1828 Definition

The fourth of the Ten Commandments (Exod 20:8–11): “Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy” — commanding the weekly setting apart of one day in seven for rest and worship, grounded in the six-day creation pattern and pointing eschatologically to the eternal Sabbath rest of God's people in the new creation.

FOURTH COMMANDMENT, n. The commandment of Exodus 20:8–11 commanding the observation of the Sabbath day — one day in seven set apart as holy rest and worship, ceasing from ordinary labor, and devoted to the public and private worship of God.

2. TWO GROUNDS: the Exodus version grounds the Sabbath in creation (Gen 2:2–3 — God rested; Exod 20:11 — therefore the LORD blessed the Sabbath day); the Deuteronomy version adds a redemptive ground (Deut 5:15 — remember you were slaves in Egypt; therefore God commanded the Sabbath to give you rest).

3. LORD'S DAY APPLICATION: the Christian church, from apostolic times, observed the first day of the week (Sunday) as the day of resurrection-worship (Acts 20:7; 1 Cor 16:2; Rev 1:10) — the Reformed tradition calling this the “Lord's Day” and applying the Fourth Commandment's substance to it as the weekly Christian Sabbath.

4. CREATION ORDINANCE: the Westminster Confession (21:7–8) and 1689 Confession (22:7–8) hold the weekly Sabbath to be a creation ordinance for all humanity — not merely a Mosaic ceremonial law — and therefore morally binding in its substance (one day in seven for worship and rest) across all ages.

5. ESCHATOLOGICAL HORIZON (Heb 4:9–11): “there remains a Sabbath rest for the people of God — for the one who has entered His rest has himself also rested from his works, as God did from His” — every Lord's Day points forward to the eternal rest of the new creation.

Key Scripture

Exod 20:8 — "Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy."

Exod 20:11 — "For in six days the LORD made the heavens and the earth, the sea, and all that is in them, and rested the seventh day. Therefore the LORD blessed the Sabbath day and hallowed it."

Gen 2:2 — "And on the seventh day God ended His work which He had done, and He rested on the seventh day from all His work which He had done."

Heb 4:9 — "So there remains a Sabbath rest for the people of God."

Modern Corruption

Modern evangelicalism has largely abandoned Sabbath observance as either legalism (antinomian reaction) or as Jewish ceremonial law fulfilled and abolished in Christ (a misreading of Hebrews that divorces the Sabbath from its creation-ordinance ground). Both positions evacuate the Fourth Commandment of binding force for the church.

expand to see more

The antinomian reading of the Fourth Commandment — that it, like all the Mosaic ceremonial law, was fulfilled in Christ and has no binding force for New Testament Christians — confuses the Sabbath's creation-ordinance ground (Gen 2:2–3, predating Moses by 2,500 years) with its ceremonial applications (Sabbath years, Jubilee, new moons, specific Mosaic penalties). What Paul declares “a shadow of things to come” (Col 2:16–17) refers to the Mosaic feast-calendar's ceremonial observances, not to the weekly creation pattern that Hebrews 4:9 explicitly says “remains” for the people of God.

Contemporary evangelicalism has in practice replaced the Lord's Day with the consumer Sunday: morning attendance at a preferred service, followed by brunch, shopping, and entertainment. The Fourth Commandment's pattern of corporate worship, ceasing from ordinary labor, family devotion, and preparation for the coming week has been dissolved by the logic of individual preference and the culture's refusal to recognize any day as categorically different from another. The church that loses the Lord's Day loses the weekly rehearsal of resurrection hope and the corporate discipline of setting time apart for God — disciplines that have historically produced the deepest wells of Sabbath joy in those who practice them faithfully.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The Hebrew shabbat (Sabbath, from shabat, to cease, rest) gives the Fourth Commandment its primary vocabulary — the weekly rest-pattern instituted at creation and re-instituted at Sinai, pointing forward through resurrection to eternal rest.

expand to see more

Hebrew shabat — to cease, stop, rest; the verbal root from which shabbat derives, used of God's rest on the seventh day (Gen 2:2) and of the Israelite's commanded cessation from labor

Hebrew shabbat — Sabbath, the seventh day; the noun for the weekly rest-day, also applied to the seventh-year fallow (Exod 23:10–11) and the Jubilee (Lev 25), all structured on the sabbatical principle

Hebrew zachar — remember; the opening verb of the Fourth Commandment (Exod 20:8) — an active, intentional recollection and ordering of life, not passive memory

Greek sabbatismos — Sabbath rest; Hebrews 4:9's unique word for the eschatological Sabbath that “remains” for the people of God — used nowhere else in the NT, underscoring its deliberate force

Christian Sabbath / Lord's Day: the apostolic and post-apostolic shift from the seventh day to the first, grounded in resurrection (Rev 1:10 — “the Lord's Day”) — the weekly commemoration of the first day of the new creation

Usage

"The Westminster Confession of Faith (21:7–8) distinguishes the moral substance of the Fourth Commandment (one day in seven, kept holy) from its ceremonial circumstance (the specific day), arguing that the moral substance is binding for all ages while the specific day was changed by apostolic authority from the seventh to the first day of the week."

"Jonathan Edwards and the Puritan tradition practiced a “double-preparation” Lord's Day: Saturday evening was given to preparing the soul for the next day's worship through prayer, Scripture reading, and meditation, so that Sunday's corporate worship was met with a heart already tuned to the Lord's frequency."

"The Heidelberg Catechism (Q&A 103) applies the Fourth Commandment to the Christian's regular attendance at the assembly of God's people, particularly to learn from the Word, use the sacraments, call upon the Lord publicly, and give Christian offerings to the poor — a comprehensive vision of Lord's Day worship as communal, sacramental, proclamatory, and charitable."
